zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review sources: Native scan, Bibliothèque nationale de France / Gallica. Secondary lexical check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, licensed CC BY 4.0 (official release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The transcription corrections and English notes are original scan-grounded review work; the lexical data and generated reading hints do not determine diplomatic spelling.

lines.note: Yuuta gotoku completes Saixoni from f432: 'as I said at the beginning'. This is running continuation text, not a repetition of the preceding page's catchword to remove.
Saishoo is glossed as a married woman. The visibly repeated Tçuma tçuma is retained as the printed Japanese explanation, not silently reduced to one word.
Saiyen denotes a garden in which vegetables are sown. Orta and ortaliça preserve the source's historical spellings without modern initial h.
Saiyuu is enjoying recreation again, explained by futatabi asobu. The Portuguese deſenfadarſe gives diversion or recreation rather than modern annoyance alone.
Vezes completes doing so twice. The final S marks the entry's written-register usage. The terminal S. is an upright written-register label.
Sajen is a pious or meritorious work. Butsuji sajen introduces an example of religious observance; Fa- begins the Portuguese infinitive fazer below.

runs.text: zer obras pias conuidando o Bonzo, & outros,

lines.note: Zer completes fazer. The pious works involve inviting the Bonzo and other people, with another action added on the following row.

The observance includes having the Foquequiǒ read. This is the sutra title embedded in Portuguese; enlargement favors the small caron over its final vowel rather than the OCR's grave, though the impression is weak.
Saji is a spoon, directly glossed by Colher. The Portuguese word is the utensil noun here, not the verb meaning to collect.
Sajiki is a raised platform or reserved viewing place, explained by tana wo shiku. Se- begins separado, describing its separation from the surrounding area.

runs.text: parado donde ſe vee o auto.

lines.note: Parado completes separado. The place is one from which a theatrical performance is seen; auto is retained as the historical Portuguese term.
This regional Sama means a window. The final X is the Ximo usage label and is visibly upright; it does not belong to the following honorific entry.

runs.text: Palaura, que ſe vſa pera honrar no cabo

lines.note: The second Sama is the honorific attached to names. The scan supports Palaura, not OCR Pulaura, and the Portuguese sentence continues with what it follows.

runs.text: dos nomes das peßoas como merce, ſenhoria,

lines.note: The suffix is placed at the end of people's names, compared with Portuguese forms of respectful address. Merce and senhoria are explanatory analogies, not Japanese words.
Tonosama is the first honorific example, rendered 'the lord Tono'. Pa- begins Padresama on the next line; its P belongs to the upright example, not to the italic Portuguese run.
Dresama completes Pa-dresama, a respectful form for a priest. The scan shows e rather than OCR o. Uyesa- starts the next honorific example and continues below.
Ma completes Uyesama. The Portuguese identifies the person as lord of the Tenca, with that Japanese political term embedded in the explanation.
This Sama means manner, form, or appearance. The scan supports Maneira and feição, not OCR Mancira and ſeição; Sama wo starts the example below.
Kayuru completes sama wo kayuru, changing one's appearance or dress. The Portuguese offers changing costume and disguising oneself as the applicable senses.

Samade means to that degree, corresponding to sahodo and 'as much as that'. Safodo is chosen for the abraded Japanese synonym; the vowel after S is weak, but the surviving traces and meaning favor a over OCR u.
Samagoshi denotes window bars or a window lattice. Grades de janella connects it with the earlier regional Sama meaning window.

runs.text: Particula que ſe vſa reprendendo, ou

lines.note: Samari is described as a particle used in rebuke or another emotional reaction continued below. The initial is visibly S, not OCR B.
Almirandoſe supplies the reaction of wonder or astonishment, retaining the printed historical form. The final B is an upright low-register label, not part of the italic explanatory word.
Samatage gives the verb for hindering or obstructing. The Portuguese begins impedir or fazer estorvo, with eſ- continued on the next row.
Toruo completes eſ-toruo, an obstruction. The short row belongs to the verbal entry and must not be merged with the following noun.
The noun Samatage is an impediment or obstruction. Its separate entry and printed estoruo spelling are retained.
Samashi denotes cooling, and the entry then introduces waking from sleep. The printed principal parts are retained, including aita, rather than replaced by modern -shita forms.
Sa-masu completes nemuri wo samasu; me wo samasu is given as an alternative. Both are explained as waking from sleep, and the Latin l separates the alternatives.
Yume wo samasu means waking from a dream. The Portuguese Acordar do sonho supplies the specific contrast with the preceding general sleep example.
Yoi wo samasu concerns recovering from intoxication. The older expression cozer ovinho is retained as printed rather than treated as literal food preparation here.
Deſembebedarſe explicitly explains sobering up and closes the preceding yoi wo samasu example. Its spelling is not modernized.
Samayoi denotes wandering or roaming without a settled course. Both printed vowel signs point upward, so ô replaces the OCR's caron in the first inflected form; the gloss continues below.
Por diversas partes completes wandering through various places. The OCR split diuer ſas is removed because the scan supports a single continuous word.
Samazama denotes many forms or manners. The tightly printed Muitasfeições is retained rather than respaced from modern expectations.
Samazamani is explicitly marked as an adverb: in many forms or ways. Latin l introduces the alternative Portuguese noun completed on the next row.
Maneiras completes the adverbial gloss, 'in many manners'. It is a short continuation, not the start of the adjective below.

Samazama no is the adjectival form, describing things of many kinds. The a after Sam is very abraded but occupies a letter position with residual ink; Samazamano is chosen rather than preserving the OCR's false word break.

runs.text: maneiras, ou feições, ou varias couſas.

lines.note: The adjective applies to many manners, appearances, or different things. This continuation completes the distinction from adverbial Samazamani.

runs.text: Hum certo peixe como raya, ou lixa. Itẽ,

lines.note: Same names a fish compared with a ray or lixa, followed by a second sense. The comparison is retained without assigning a modern species, and Itẽ introduces the use of its skin below.

runs.text: Apelle deſte peixe, q̃ ſerue de cobrir os punhos

lines.note: The fish's skin serves to cover sword grips. The visible u restores ſerue rather than OCR ſerae; the close setting Apelle is retained.
The covering is applied to the Catana's grips or to the sheath. Catana is the Japanese sword term embedded in Portuguese, and abainha retains the printed close spacing.
Same uma denotes a horse described as having white eyes. The gloss states that visible characteristic, without warrant for a more specific modern breed or color diagnosis.
The verb Same means a hot thing cooling down. It is distinct from the fish noun and the horse expression despite the identical opening letters.
A further sense is waking from sleep. Me ga same- begins the example, with the past form completed on the next line.
Ta completes me ga sameta, 'awoke from sleep'. Kokoro ga sa- introduces a figurative example concerning the heart or inward disposition.

runs.text: Per met. Esfriarſe o coração. i. Dei-

lines.note: Meta completes kokoro ga sameta. The metaphor is the heart cooling, or losing fervor; the scan restores Esfriarſe from OCR Es foiarſe, and Dei- continues into Deixar below.

Xar completes Deixar o feruor, losing fervor. Sake no yoi ga sameta then introduces sobering up after alcohol; feruor and ſameta replace the OCR's vowel and consonant confusions. Its explanation begins in the next column.

runs.text: Deixar de eſtar bebado, ou eſfriarſe do calor

lines.note: This translates sake no yoi ga sameta from the previous column: no longer being drunk or cooling from the heat of wine. The physical indentation is restored to match this continuing gloss.
Do vinho completes the alcohol-related explanation. The short continuation closes the verb entry before Same zame begins.

runs.text: Aduer. Modo de chorar muito, ou

lines.note: Same zame is an adverbial expression for copious crying. The Portuguese introduces both the action and the flow of tears elaborated on the next row.

runs.text: correrem as lagrimasfio em fio. Vt,

lines.note: The tears run fio em fio, in continuous streams. The tight lagrimasfio setting is retained, and Same- starts the example across the line break.
Zame to naku completes same-zame to naku, crying in that abundant manner. The Portuguese restates the mode of crying.

runs.text: Bainha cuberta de pelle de lixa.

lines.note: Samezaya is a scabbard covered with the fish skin described in the left column. The final word is lixa, with a visible a, not OCR lixo.

Samishi, suru denotes treating someone with contempt or making little of them, not the unrelated modern adjective for loneliness. The printed end mark is a division hyphen in eſcar-, continued by necer below.
Necer completes eſcar-necer, to scorn. Buke no tomogara Cugue- begins an example contrasting members of the warrior group with court nobles.

Wo samishi completes the Japanese statement about scorning the court nobles. The Portuguese says the soldiers did not esteem them; the OCR's internal space in ſoldados is removed after scan comparison.
Vão completes eſtima-uão. Cungues is the Portuguese-inflected form for the court nobles within the gloss and is retained despite differing from Japanese Cugue above.
Samidare is rain of the fifth month, explained by goguat no ame. The checked t in Goguatno is preserved rather than expanded to modern gatsu.

runs.text: ta lũa, ou mes que chamão Nagaxi.

lines.note: The fifth lunar month is specified, and Nagaxi is supplied as another name associated with this rain. The term occurs within the Portuguese explanation, not as a new entry.
Samo is an adverb meaning thus or so. Samo are is the first example, with Se- beginning its Portuguese translation on the next line.
Ja completes Se-ja aßi, 'let it be so'. Samo araba are follows as a second example, whose translation begins 'let it be as'.
Quer que for completes the concessive 'however it may be'. Samo omoshiroi then illustrates an exclamatory use expressing strong appreciation or interest.

runs.text: couſa pera ver, ou tam apraziuel!

lines.note: The Portuguese exclaims over something worth seeing or very pleasing. The visible tall final mark is retained as an exclamation mark rather than the OCR's period.

runs.text: O ter, ou fazer frio. Item, couſa fria.

lines.note: Samui covers feeling cold, cold weather, and something being cold. The Portuguese distinguishes those constructions without changing the Japanese headword.
Samui jibun is a cold time or season, glossed Tempo frio. The example remains one physical line.
Samusa is the nominal derivative, coldness. Its indented standalone row belongs to the preceding adjective's forms, not to page furniture.
Samuu is the adverbial form printed with a caron over u. Like Samusa, it is a separate short body row linked to Samui.

runs.text: Couſa fria, ou o ter frio.

lines.note: Samumi is labeled poetic and glossed as coldness or feeling cold. P is visibly upright and identifies register rather than a word in the Portuguese gloss.
Samushiro is the poetic form equated with mushiro, a mat. The upright P and explanatory i are kept outside the italic Portuguese definition.
San is the number three, explained by mitsu. The scan shows capital S, not the OCR's X; no enlarged initial or new section heading is present.
This San concerns calculation, with kangayuru as its Japanese explanation. The scan has San rather than OCR Sani; the Portuguese identifies numerical accounts or arithmetic.
San wo oku is doing a calculation or reckoning. The initial v in voqu is preserved as part of the historical spelling of oku.
The next San is childbirth, explained by umu. San wo tayasuu suru gives the expression for an easy delivery; the printed round s and vowel mark in tayasǔ are retained.
The first example is translated as giving birth easily. San no himo wo toku follows as another childbirth expression, literally evoking the loosening of a cord.
Parir supplies the second example's meaning, to give birth. The single-word continuation is retained as its own physical row.

runs.text: Verſo, ou eſcritura que declara a pintura,

lines.note: This San is a verse or inscription that explains a picture. The sentence continues with other possible subjects and its praising function below.
The inscription can concern another object and magnifies or praises it. This completes the laudatory-text sense, distinct from the counting rods in the next entry.

runs.text: Huns paozinhos com que deitão ſortes,

lines.note: The following San denotes little sticks used in casting lots. The Portuguese goes on to mention their arithmetic use on the next line.

runs.text: ou fazem cõtas: propriamẽte ſe chamão ſãgui.

lines.note: The sticks are also used for calculations and are properly called sangi. The scan's colon after cõtas is restored; ſãgui retains its nasal abbreviation and is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese.
San wo midasu means mixing or scattering the rods. The printed pao zinhos spacing is kept rather than normalized to the undivided form in the later comparison.
Shigai wa san wo chiraita gotoku de at- compares dead bodies with scattered rods. Chiraita is the historical past form of chirasu, not a defective modern chirashita spelling.
Ta completes atta. Midaita gotoku is offered as an alternative phrasing; midaita similarly preserves historical s-row i-onbin. The Portuguese starts its comparison with the dead bodies below.
The dead bodies were strewn and mixed together. Como introduces the comparison with the disordered divination rods on the next line.

runs.text: paozinhos das ſortes, que eſtão baralhados ſem

lines.note: The comparison is with lot-casting sticks mixed without order. The scan supports the h of paozinhos rather than OCR b; sem continues into ordem below.
Ordem completes the disordered-rods comparison. San wo oku is then introduced in its divination sense, rendered as casting lots.

runs.text: pera adiuinhar algũa couſa como fazẽ os gẽtios,

lines.note: The lots are cast to divine something, ascribed to the practice of the people called gentios. The printed abbreviation marks in algũa, fazẽ, and gẽtios are retained.
Ou fazer contas adds arithmetic as the other use of the rods. This closes the long entry before the Buddhist term Sanacudǒ begins.
San'akudoo is glossed as three infernal states, with jigoku and gaki beginning the list. The dictionary's own classification is preserved rather than recast as a modern doctrinal taxonomy.
Chikushoo completes the list of the three unfavorable states. This short Japanese continuation belongs to the preceding enumeration, not a new headword.

runs.text: Adu. Sem tirar nem por, ou nem

lines.note: Sanagara is an adverb meaning exactly as it is, without subtracting or adding anything. The Portuguese gives that intactness sense before restating it below.
Mais nem menos completes 'neither more nor less'. It reinforces the exact-equivalence sense of Sanagara.
Sanae is the poetic word for rice seedlings, explained by ine no nae. The P label is upright; the acute over the final vowel of eſtá is read from the local mark rather than normalized from the draft.

runs.text: nacido de pouco em erua pera ſe deſpor.

lines.note: The rice has recently sprouted as young green growth and is ready to be planted out. The damaged word reads erua, not eraa; the source retains nacido and deſpor as historical Portuguese forms.

Sanbyoo introduces three illnesses. Raibyoo corresponds to the leprosy gloss at the start of f434; its initial R and the headword's San replace garbled OCR. Cutçu- continues as chi on f434, while the intervening bottom catchword is recorded separately.
The catchword visibly has ch followed by a comma. It anticipates chi, on bnf-f0434, but no separate i is securely visible, so that expected letter is not supplied.
